title: Disaster Recovery Strategies: RPO & RTO
summary: Backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby and active-active, and how to pick one.
tldr: **RPO** = how much data you can lose (time since the last good copy). **RTO** = how long you can be down. Read both numbers first, then pick the *cheapest* strategy that meets them.
The four strategies, cheapest to most expensive: **backup and restore** → **pilot light** → **warm standby** → **multi-site active-active**.
The difference between pilot light and warm standby is the app tier: pilot light keeps only *data* live in the DR Region; warm standby also runs a *scaled-down, working* copy of the app.
Servers you can't rebuild (legacy, custom OS config, on premises) with an RPO of seconds → **AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS)**.

keyFacts.text: **Backup and restore**: RPO and RTO in hours. Copy backups to another Region (AWS Backup copy rules) and rebuild from IaC when disaster strikes.
**Pilot light**: data replicated continuously (cross-Region read replica, Global Database), AMIs and templates ready, but app servers stay switched off until failover.
**Warm standby**: a smaller but fully working stack already serves health checks in the DR Region. Scale it out and switch DNS on failover.
**Multi-site active-active**: every Region takes live traffic. Write locally with DynamoDB global tables, or write to one Region with Aurora Global Database.
**Elastic Disaster Recovery** replicates servers at block level into a low-cost staging area and launches full-size recovery instances only for drills or failover.

traps: **Multi-AZ is not DR for a Regional outage.** A Multi-AZ standby lives in the same Region.
Pilot light and warm standby both keep a live database copy. If the question says no app servers may run, it is pilot light; if a small app fleet already runs, it is warm standby.
Don't pay for active-active or a warm standby when the stated RPO/RTO is hours. The question usually asks for the *most cost-effective* option that still meets the numbers.
Snapshots or DLM copies every 15 minutes can't give an RPO of seconds. Continuous replication (DRS, Global Database, global tables) can.
Aurora Global Database write forwarding still sends writes to one primary Region; when that Region fails you must promote a secondary, so it is not multi-writer.
Replication copies corruption and deletes too. Keep point-in-time backups alongside any pilot light, warm standby or active-active design.
Service quotas are per Region. A DR Region with low vCPU or other quotas can't scale to production size, so raise the quotas before you need them and check them in DR tests.
Remember the dependencies: AMIs, KMS keys, secrets and network routes must all exist in the DR Region, not only the data.

sections.heading: Reading a DR question in 20 seconds
sections.body:
1. Underline the **RPO** and the **RTO**.
2. Check what may run in the DR Region (nothing, data only, small app tier, full app).
3. Check whether the source can be rebuilt from IaC. If not, think **Elastic Disaster Recovery** or AMIs.
4. Pick the cheapest strategy that still meets both numbers, then add the routing (Route 53 failover, ARC routing controls, Global Accelerator) and the data replication that strategy needs.
